title: Maximum Average Subarray I
description: Brute force to optimized: re-summing every fixed-size window versus sliding one running sum forward in O(1) per step.

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, find a contiguous subarray of length exactly k that has the maximum average value, and return that average.

blocks.caption: Slide a fixed-size window across nums, tracking the maximum sum seen

blocks.text: Given an integer array nums and an integer k, find a contiguous subarray of length exactly k that has the maximum average value, and return that average.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Rolling Average of Your Last k Exam Scores
blocks.text: Like tracking the average of your most recent k exam scores: when a new exam happens, you drop the oldest score and add the newest one, instead of re-averaging every score from the very beginning each time.

blocks.caption: Drop the oldest score, add the newest, and the rolling average updates instantly

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Windows of length 4: [1,12,-5,-6], [12,-5,-6,50], [-5,-6,50,3]","sums 2, 51, 42","Every possible length-4 contiguous subarray is considered"],["Answer","12.75","The best window sums to 51, and 51 / 4 = 12.75"]]}

blocks.text: With only one element and a window size of 1, the only possible average is the element itself, 5.0.
When every element is negative, the maximum average is still well defined, it is simply the least negative window found, since some window must be chosen.
Before recomputing every window's sum from scratch, notice that neighboring windows of a FIXED size overlap almost entirely.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A window of length k moving forward by one position loses exactly its leftmost element and gains exactly one new rightmost element; everything else stays identical.

Observation 2: This means the new window's sum can be computed from the previous window's sum using just one subtraction and one addition, instead of re-adding all k elements.

Observation 3: Build the very first window's sum once, directly, then slide forward one position at a time, updating the running sum incrementally.

Observation 4: Track the maximum running sum seen across every window position, and divide by k only once at the very end to get the average.

Whenever a problem asks about every FIXED-size contiguous window of an array, maintaining a running sum that updates in O(1) per slide, instead of recomputing from scratch, turns an O(n*k) approach into an O(n) one.
This "drop the oldest, add the newest" update is the core idea behind every fixed-size sliding window problem, and it directly motivates the optimized approach below.
For every possible starting position, sum all k elements of that window directly, and track the best sum found.

items: Loop over every valid starting position for a length-k window.
For each starting position, sum all k elements of that window directly, then compare against the best sum found so far.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: The inner loop always sums exactly k elements starting from the current position, directly matching the problem's fixed window length.
The division by k happens only once, at the very end, after the best SUM (not average) has already been found, avoiding repeated floating-point division inside the loops.
maxSum starts at negative infinity so that even an all-negative array correctly updates it on the very first window.

blocks.text: Every window's true sum is computed directly, so the correct maximum average is always found.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n * k), since each of the roughly n windows re-sums k elements.
Space: O(1) extra.
Limitation: re-summing k elements for every one of the roughly n windows repeats almost all of the same additions across neighboring windows, since they share k-1 elements.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force redoes nearly identical work for every window, since sliding forward by one position only changes two elements: the one leaving on the left and the one entering on the right. Instead of re-summing all k elements every time, compute the first window's sum once, then update it incrementally for every subsequent window using a single subtraction and a single addition. This turns O(n * k) work into O(n) work overall.

Compute the sum of the first k elements directly, once. Then, for each subsequent position, subtract the element leaving the window and add the element entering it, updating the running sum in O(1). Track the maximum running sum seen, and divide by k at the very end.
Maintain a running window sum, updated incrementally as the window slides one position at a time.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass.
Space: O(1) extra.

Two consecutive length-k windows differ by exactly one element on each side: the window sliding forward loses its leftmost element and gains one new rightmost element, while every element in between is shared by both windows. Subtracting the leaving element and adding the entering element therefore produces the exact same result as summing the new window directly, without ever re-touching the k-2 shared elements.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What happens"],"rows":[["Sliding forward by one position","Subtract nums[i - k], add nums[i], where i is the new rightmost index"],["The very first window","No sliding has happened yet, so it is summed directly once as the starting point"]]}

items: The first window's sum is computed directly, in its own short loop, since there is no previous window to slide from yet.
Every subsequent window's sum is derived from the previous one using exactly one subtraction and one addition, keeping each update at O(1).
The division by k is deferred until after the best SUM has been found, avoiding unnecessary floating-point operations inside the main loop.

blocks.text: Whenever a problem needs a value (sum, average, max, etc.) over every fixed-size window of an array, maintaining a running result that updates in O(1) per slide is almost always possible, and turns an O(n*k) brute force into an O(n) solution.

items: Dividing by k inside the loop on every window instead of once at the end, which is both wasteful and can introduce unnecessary floating-point rounding earlier than needed.
Forgetting to initialize the running best sum to negative infinity (or the first window's own sum), which could silently produce a wrong answer if the array contains only negative numbers.
Off-by-one errors in the subtract/add indices when sliding the window, such as subtracting nums[i - k + 1] instead of nums[i - k].

blocks.content: {"headers":["Edge case","Expected behavior"],"rows":[["k equals nums.length","There is only one possible window, the entire array, so the answer is simply its own average"],["All elements are negative","The maximum average is still correctly found, as the least negative window"]]}

items: Explicitly mention the "drop the oldest, add the newest" update out loud, since recognizing this is the entire insight behind every fixed-size sliding window problem.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Find the best sum, average, or count over every window of a FIXED size k" points toward a fixed-size sliding window: build the first window directly, then slide by subtracting the leaving element and adding the entering one.

items: How would this change if the window size were variable instead of fixed? A variable-size sliding window would be needed instead, growing and shrinking based on some condition rather than always staying exactly k elements wide.
What if you needed the k windows with the highest averages, not just the single best one? A min-heap of size k could track the top k running sums seen so far, instead of a single running maximum.

How would you handle this if nums were streamed one element at a time, rather than given as a complete array upfront? The same sliding window update still works incrementally, needing only the last k elements in a queue-like buffer.

The same fixed-size sliding window update reappears in problems like Maximum Number of Vowels in a Substring of Given Length and Substrings of Size Three with Distinct Characters, both elsewhere in this category.
Contrasts directly with variable-size sliding window problems (like Minimum Size Subarray Sum), where the window's length itself changes based on a condition, rather than staying fixed.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n * k) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (sliding window sum): O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: Fixed-size sliding window, sliding by subtracting the leaving element and adding the entering one
Core Idea: Two consecutive length-k windows share k-1 elements, so the new window's sum can be derived from the previous one in O(1)
Time: O(n)
Space: O(1)
Most Important Observation: A window sliding forward by one position only changes at its two edges, letting the running sum update incrementally instead of being recomputed
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: Drop the oldest, add the newest, keep the best
